extracted.intended_audience: people submitting to The New Yorker cartoon caption contest; humor writers aiming for New Yorker tone
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing winning captions for The New Yorker cartoon caption contest: how to match the magazine's taste (dry, intellectual, subtle) rather than write the objectively funniest line. Emphasizes 'theory of mind' style and tonal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterintuitive Thesis — win vs. funniest
rubrics_metrics.description: "You are not trying to submit the funniest caption; you are trying to win The New Yorker's caption contest. Humor and victory are different matters entirely."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-rule: prioritize what the New Yorker audience/editors reward over what you personally find funniest. Align with the magazine's sensibility rather than maximizing broad laugh intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Mind Captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Stat: 136 of 145 winners (94%) are "theory of mind" captions. These require the reader to project intents or beliefs into the minds of the cartoon's characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form: give a character's interior reasoning that recasts the absurd scene. This is a dominant structural strategy for winners — supply a plausible mental state or motive that reframes the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mild Chuckle Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: "Your caption should elicit, at best, a mild chuckle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anything that produces a loud or belly laugh; such overtly funny lines can discomfit the New Yorker reader. Aim for subtle amusement that signals intelligence and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it ascribe a thought/belief/intent to a character (theory of mind)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the caption give a character an interior thought, belief, or intent that explains or reframes the scene?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the single most important evaluative test — winners usually offer an internal monologue or motive that makes the absurdity psychologically believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is it more wry than laugh-out-loud?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the tone wry (dry, ironic, understated) rather than designed to provoke an audible laugh?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arch intelligence and understatement. Avoid overt punchlines, broad jokes, or slapstick-style humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it treat the absurd scene as mundane?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the caption downplay the absurdity by treating the strange or surreal elements as ordinary?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframing the image as normal or procedural often increases the wry effect. Downplaying the weirdness invites a smirk of recognition rather than incredulous laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it appeal to the New Yorker reader's self-image (intelligent, urbane)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the caption speak to the magazine's readership by being self-aware, intellectualized, or demonstrating urbane sensibility?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful captions flatter or reflect the New Yorker reader's perceived values — subtle wit, cultural literacy, and a dry point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is it short, dignified, dry?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the caption concise and composed in a dignified, dry register?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of words and a formal or restrained voice help the caption feel like it belongs in the magazine. Avoid overly chatty, crude, or exuberant phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: What wins — combined checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions that ascribe a believable inner state; downplay the absurdity (treat it as mundane); are wry rather than slapstick; and are self-aware, intellectualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This synthesized checklist collects the recurring features of past winners: psychological reframing + understatement + intellectual tone. Use it as a composite guide when choosing/editing a submission.
